section.title: ISO installer
section.para: Agama installer is deployed as a regular application which can be installed and run on a local system. However, the most expected way of using Agama is by running it on a live ISO image.

section.title: Sources
section.para: The Live ISO sources are maintained in the Agama’s repository live/ subdirectory. See more details in the live/README.md documentation.

section.title: Live ISO requirements
section.para: A live ISO for running Agama should provide the following software:

listitem.para: Hardware drivers.
Agama installer and related tools (lvm, cryptsetup, NetworkManager, etc).
A browser to locally render the Agama web UI.
Optionally, repository packages of the products to install.

note.para: If no browser is included, then the installation has to be remotely performed by using a browser from another machine. This would be the typical case for s390x installations.

warning.para: These days the packages repositories are not included, so the installation requires Internet connection to download the packages of the product to install.

section.title: Agama Live ISO (only for development and testing)
section.para: The Agama project provides a live ISO image for testing purposes and it is intended to be used for developers only. It has some limitations and it is not optimized for production usage.

listitem.para: The live ISO is based on openSUSE Tumbleweed.
Allows installing both SUSE and openSUSE products.
Weighs around 1 GiB.
Contains Agama installer and tools, and hardware drivers.

para.emphasis: Includes Firefox (except for ppc64le and s390x).
Does not include packages from product repositories.

listitem.para: Supported archs: x86_64, aarch64, ppc64le and s390x.
2 GiB of RAM memory
Internet connection to download packages of the product to install.
Around 10 GiB of disk size, although it depends on the selected product to install.

section.title: Experimental self-update

warning.para: This feature is experimental and untested!

section.para: The Agama packages on the Live ISO can be automatically updated from the OBS Devel project.

listitem.para: Use the inst.self_update boot parameter to run the self-update automatically during boot.
Or run the agama-self-update script anytime later in a running Live system.

note.para: After updating the packages the Agama servers need to be restarted. This will reset all you current Agama settings, you will need to start from scratch!

section.title: The access password
section.para: Because the ISO image is built publicly we cannot use any predefined password as everybody would know that and for attackers it would be really trivial to hack your running installer.
That means you have to provide our own password. If none is specified then Agama generates a random password and prints it on the console after boot.

section.title: Using a custom password
section.para: There are several ways how to specify your custom password, each of them might be suitable for a different use case.

section.title: Boot command line
section.para: You can define the password directly on the boot command line. There are two options:

listitem.para: Use live.password=<password> with a plain text password.
Use live.password_hash=<password_hash> with a hashed password. This is more secure than using a plaintext password.

The disadvantage is that the hashed password is quite long and is not easy to type it into the boot prompt manually. It makes sense in environments where you can prepare the boot parameters in advance like in PXE boot or some virtual machines.
See more details about creating a hashed password below.

section.title: Interactive input
section.para: You can enter your password during boot in an interactive session. Again, there are two options:

listitem.para: Use live.password_dialog boot option to start an interactive dialog during the boot process. This uses a nice dialog for entering and confirming the password. However, in some situations the full screen dialog might not be displayed correctly or some messages might be displayed over it. In that case you might use the Ctrl+L key shortcut to refresh the screen. If it still does not work then try using the other option below.

Use live.password_systemd boot option to ask for the password in a simple prompt. This is similar to the option above, but the advantage is that this solution does not use a full screen dialog but a single line prompt so it should work better in special environments like a serial console.

section.para: The Agama and the SSH server are not started until a password is configured. This avoid using the default password from the medium accidentally.

section.title: Injecting the default password into the ISO image
section.para: Another option is to inject your custom hashed password directly into the ISO image. The advantage is than you can easily use the same image for installing multiple machines and you do not need to configure anything during the boot.
To inject a new password into the ISO run:
section.programlisting: # replace the agama.iso name with your image name tagmedia --add-tag "live_password=$((openssl passwd -6) | base64 -w 0)" agama.iso
section.para: It will interactively ask for a password then it will be hashed using the SHA512 algorithm, encoded to the Base64 encoding and appended to the application area in the ISO file. If you want to update the password then just the same command again, it will overwrite the existing password.
See the Creating a Hashed Password section below if you want to use a different hashing algorithm than SHA512.
To check all tags present in an ISO file use this command:
section.programlisting: # replace the agama.iso name with your image name tagmedia agama.iso
section.para: If you want to remove the password setting from the ISO image then run:
section.programlisting: # replace the agama.iso name with your image name tagmedia --remove-tag live_password agama.iso

danger.para: The image usually already contains some other tags, like the checksums for verifying the medium integrity. Do not touch them!

section.title: Random password as a fallback
section.para: When no password is specified or entering the password interactively was canceled by the user then Agama generates a random password and prints it on the console.

section.title: Password priority
section.para: The password setting priority is following (from highest priority to the lowest):

listitem.para: Password entered interactively during the boot process
Password entered on the boot command line
Default password from the ISO image meta data
A random password is generated as a fallback

section.title: Creating a Hashed Password
section.para: There are several ways how to create a password hash, here we will mention two tools.

Each tool allows to select the encryption method to use. To check the details about all encryption methods see man 5 crypt, it lists the encryption methods sorted by their strength so you can check which methods are recommended and which ones should be avoided.

section.title: Mkpasswd
section.para: You can use the mkpasswd tool from the whois package. It offers a lot of encryption methods, see the mkpasswd -m help for the list.
By default it uses the strongest method available so in most cases you just run
and then enter the password on the command line prompt.

section.title: OpenSSL
section.para: Alternatively you can use the openssl passwd command from the openSSL package. It offers less encryption methods but on the other hand it should be basically installed in every system.

warning.para: By default it uses a weak encryption method (DES or MD5 depending on the OpenSSL version) so you should always provide an additional encryption method parameter to select a stronger encryption!

section.para: To create a SHA512 hash for your password run
and then enter the password on the command line prompt.
For less strong SHA256 hash use the -5 option, the other encryption methods should be avoided.
